opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of what we do at Berkeley starts with looking at trends that are pretty predictable, at least in direction, and asking what breaks or what becomes possible if they continue for a few more years.

With Spark, around 2009, a few things were happening at once. Hadoop and MapReduce were the dominant way to process big data, and they were great for batch jobs where you read a lot of data from disk, do some work, and write it back. But people increasingly wanted to do machine learning, and machine learning algorithms are iterative. You go over the same data again and again. With MapReduce, every iteration meant reading from disk and writing back to disk, which was very slow.

At the same time, if you looked at memory, it was getting cheaper and the capacity per machine was growing quickly. And when we looked at actual workloads, in many cases the working set people cared about, the data they queried or trained on, could fit in the aggregate memory of a cluster, even when the total data stored was much larger. So the opportunity was clear: if you can keep the data in memory across iterations, you can be ten or a hundred times faster.

The hard part, and where the research was, was fault tolerance. In a distributed system, machines fail, and memory is volatile. The traditional approach is to replicate data or checkpoint it, but that's expensive and defeats much of the purpose. Matei came up with the idea of resilient distributed datasets, where instead of replicating the data, you remember the lineage, the sequence of transformations that produced it. If you lose a partition, you recompute just that piece. That made in-memory processing practical at scale.

So the general pattern is: identify a trend that's going to continue, like cheaper memory or more data or more compute demand from AI. Then find the applications that are pushing on the limits of existing systems, and figure out the new abstraction that lets people take advantage of the trend. We saw the same thing later with Ray. Machine learning workloads were becoming more diverse and dynamic, models were growing, and you needed a general way to distribute Python applications across many machines. It's the same recipe: secular trend, an emerging workload that existing systems serve poorly, and a simple abstraction that hides the complexity.

And one more thing that matters a lot: we try to stay very close to users. Early Spark users were people in our lab doing machine learning, and companies we talked to. That feedback tells you whether the trend you're betting on is actually showing up in real problems.

r001.rationale: It links cheaper, growing memory with increasingly iterative machine-learning workloads and explains how their mismatch with disk-based MapReduce created an opportunity for in-memory processing.

r002.rationale: It says the relevant working set could exceed one machine’s memory but fit across a cluster, without explaining that data growth outpaces single-machine capacity.

r003.rationale: It says queried or trained working sets can fit in cluster memory despite a larger stored dataset, but does not say those queries are limited to recent data.

r004.rationale: It recommends identifying trends likely to continue and finding applications that existing systems serve poorly, so the research opportunity grows with those trends.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I actually tell my students a lot, because I think it's the single most useful thing you can do in systems research. If you look at the history of our field, most of the big ideas were not somebody being incredibly clever in a vacuum. They were somebody noticing that the underlying technology had shifted, and that the systems we were all using had been designed for a world that no longer existed.

With Spark, the trend was very simple: memory was getting cheap, and it was getting cheap fast. When we started, around 2009, 2010, you could put something like 64, 128 gigabytes in a commodity server for not very much money. And at the same time, the data people actually wanted to analyze wasn't growing nearly that fast. If you looked at what companies were really doing with Hadoop, the typical job was touching maybe a few hundred gigabytes, maybe a few terabytes. So you had this cluster of, say, 50 or 100 machines, and the aggregate memory of that cluster could hold the entire working set. That was a very different situation from the one Google was in when they designed MapReduce, where the data was so large relative to memory that of course you had to stream everything off disk.

So the question becomes almost obvious once you see it: if the data fits in memory, why are we writing it to disk after every stage? And then the second thing we noticed was on the workload side. People were starting to do iterative computations, machine learning, graph algorithms, interactive queries. These are exactly the workloads where MapReduce was terrible, because every iteration is a full round trip through HDFS. So you had a hardware trend and a workload trend pointing in the same direction. When that happens, that's when you should pay attention.

The hard part, honestly, is not spotting the trend. Everybody knew memory was getting cheaper. The hard part is asking what the implication is, and being willing to believe that the implication is big enough to redesign the system from scratch rather than patch the old one. A lot of people looked at the same facts and said, okay, let's add a cache to Hadoop. And we said, no, if memory is the primary storage, you need a different abstraction, you need to think about fault tolerance differently, because you can't afford to replicate in memory the way you replicate on disk. That's where RDDs and lineage came from. The trend tells you where to look. It doesn't tell you the answer.

And I would say the same pattern applies today. If you look at what's happening with GPUs, or with the cost of running large models, the question I'm always asking is: what assumption baked into our current systems is about to become false?

r001.rationale: It describes both a hardware trend (cheaper memory) and a workload trend (iterative and interactive analytics) pointing toward a research opportunity.

r002.rationale: It says data was not growing as fast as memory and that a cluster could hold the working set; it does not explain that data outgrowing single-machine capacity creates the need for distributed processing.

r003.rationale: It says typical jobs touched hundreds of gigabytes or terabytes and could fit in cluster memory, but does not tie feasibility to queries being limited to recent data despite a larger stored dataset.

r004.rationale: It advises watching for assumptions that may become false, but does not recommend choosing problems whose importance will increase as secular trends develop.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful approach is to look at technology trends and ask which assumptions in existing systems are going to stop being true. In systems research, you’re often building something that will take several years to mature, so you want to solve a problem that will become more important over that period.

For in-memory processing, the observation was that memory capacity was increasing, and across a cluster you could keep substantial datasets in memory. At the same time, workloads were becoming more iterative. In machine learning, for example, you repeatedly operate on the same data. If you read that data from disk on every iteration, you pay that cost over and over.

That suggests an opportunity, but it doesn’t give you the whole system. You still have to ask: How do you distribute the computation? What happens when a machine fails? How do you make this easy to program? The research opportunity is in making that hardware trend useful through the right abstractions.

So I would look for a combination: a technology trend that changes what is possible, and a workload that benefits from that change. Where those two meet is often a good place to start.

r001.rationale: It connects rising memory capacity with increasingly iterative workloads and identifies their intersection as a research opportunity.

r002.rationale: It says substantial datasets could fit in memory across a cluster, but does not explain that data is growing faster than single-machine capacity.

r003.rationale: It does not mention analytics queries being limited to recent data as a reason in-memory processing is feasible.

r004.rationale: It recommends solving problems that will become more important over the several years a systems project takes to mature.

sol-6.1.text:
I like to look at technology trends and ask which assumptions in existing systems are going to stop being true. Hardware changes continuously, but software often carries assumptions from when it was designed. That gap can create a research opportunity.

For example, memory capacity was increasing, and the aggregate memory of a cluster could hold more and more interesting datasets. At the same time, iterative workloads, such as machine learning, were becoming more important. If you repeatedly process the same data, writing it to disk and reading it back at every step becomes very expensive. So the question was: can we keep that data in memory across computations while preserving the fault tolerance you need in a distributed system?

The opportunity wasn’t simply that memory was getting cheaper. It was the combination of a hardware trend and workloads that could benefit from it. You want to identify that intersection, then find the technical problem that prevents people from taking advantage of it.

r001.rationale: It describes the opportunity as the intersection of increasing memory capacity and growing iterative workloads, where assumptions in existing systems may no longer hold.

r002.rationale: It mentions aggregate cluster memory, but does not explain that data growth exceeds single-machine capacity or that this creates a need for distributed processing.

r003.rationale: It discusses repeatedly processing the same data in memory, but not queries limited to recent data relative to a much larger stored dataset.

r004.rationale: It recommends finding the intersection of trends and a technical obstacle, but does not say to choose problems whose importance will increase as the trends develop.
